scope: all AI systems, with a risk-based tiering (banned practices, high-risk, limited-risk transparency duties, general-purpose AI models); binding across all 27 EU member states
enforcement_mechanism: yes — national market-surveillance authorities plus a new EU AI Office; fines up to 7% of global annual revenue (or €35m) for banned-practice violations, up to 3% for other breaches
effective_date_or_status: Entered into force 1 Aug 2024; banned practices + AI literacy rules applied from 2 Feb 2025; general-purpose AI model rules from 2 Aug 2025; most other rules (incl. enforcement/penalties) from 2 Aug 2026; high-risk system rules from 2 Dec 2027 (an 'AI Digital Omnibus' package agreed May 2026 pushed some high-risk deadlines back further)
plain_language_summary: The EU is the first place in the world with a real, binding AI law. It bans a few dangerous uses of AI outright, and for 'high-risk' uses like hiring or credit-scoring tools, companies must test and register the systems before selling them. Fines for breaking the rules can reach 7% of a company's worldwide revenue. It's being rolled out in stages through 2027, and some deadlines were just pushed back in 2026.

scope: all AI systems; principles-level guidance for governments and companies, not enforceable rules
enforcement_mechanism: no — voluntary principles with no fines or licensing; OECD tracks country policies via the OECD.AI Policy Observatory but has no enforcement power
effective_date_or_status: Adopted 2019, substantively updated May 2024 to add generative AI, safety, and misinformation provisions; endorsed by 47 countries/jurisdictions as of the 2024 update
plain_language_summary: This is a shared set of values — like 'AI should be safe, fair, and transparent' — that 47 countries have agreed to aim for. It's not a law and nobody can be fined for ignoring it, but it shapes how many countries write their own AI rules.

key_instruments: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS 225)
scope: AI systems used by public authorities and private actors, focused on human rights/democracy/rule-of-law impacts; open to non-European countries too
enforcement_mechanism: intended yes once in force (first-ever legally binding international AI treaty) — but not yet in force; each ratifying country sets its own enforcement/oversight body domestically
effective_date_or_status: Opened for signature 5 Sept 2024; needs 5 ratifications (incl. 3 Council of Europe member states) to enter into force; as of 7 Sept 2026 only the EU has ratified (15 May 2026) — not yet in force
plain_language_summary: This would be the world's first binding international AI treaty covering human rights, but it's stuck in the starting gate: countries have to formally ratify it before it counts, and so far (as of late 2026) only the EU itself has actually done so, even though over 20 countries including the UK, US, and Switzerland have signed on in principle.

key_instruments: UNGA Resolution on 'Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy AI' (March 2024); Global Digital Compact (Sept 2024, part of the Pact for the Future); UNGA Resolution A/RES/79/325 (Aug 2025) creating the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and Global Dialogue on AI Governance; separate Dec 2024 resolution on military AI
scope: global, all AI systems at a high level — mostly institution-building and shared principles rather than rules for specific systems
enforcement_mechanism: no — these are UN resolutions and compacts with no binding force and no penalties; the new Scientific Panel produces research/assessments, not enforcement
effective_date_or_status: Resolutions adopted March 2024, Sept 2024, Dec 2024, and Aug 2025; the Scientific Panel and Global Dialogue on AI Governance are newly-established bodies as of 2025, still standing up
plain_language_summary: The UN has gotten nearly every country in the world to agree, on paper, that AI should be safe and beneficial, and has just set up a new expert panel and a global forum to study AI risks together. None of this creates enforceable rules — it's diplomacy and shared research, not law.

key_instruments: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems (Oct 2023) + Comprehensive Policy Framework; OECD-run reporting framework launched Feb 2025
scope: advanced/frontier general-purpose AI systems developed by large AI companies, not AI generally
enforcement_mechanism: no legal enforcement — voluntary code of conduct; companies self-report against it via an OECD-hosted monitoring framework (first reports due April 2025)
effective_date_or_status: Code of Conduct agreed and endorsed by G7 leaders Oct-Dec 2023; carried forward under Italy's 2024 G7 presidency; OECD monitoring/reporting framework went live Feb 2025 with rolling company reports
plain_language_summary: The G7 countries got major AI companies to voluntarily sign a code of good conduct for their most powerful AI systems and to self-report on how they're following it. There's no fine or punishment if a company doesn't comply — it relies on public pressure and peer tracking.

key_instruments: ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (Feb 2024) + Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics — Generative AI (Jan 2025)
scope: all AI systems at a regional guidance level, with a generative-AI-specific expansion; applies across ASEAN's 10 member states as voluntary guidance, not a bloc-wide law
enforcement_mechanism: no — voluntary guide; individual ASEAN member states (e.g. Singapore) may separately have their own binding or non-binding rules, tracked in their own country rows
effective_date_or_status: Original guide issued Feb 2024; expanded generative-AI version issued Jan 2025
plain_language_summary: Southeast Asia's 10 countries agreed on a shared voluntary rulebook for trustworthy AI, covering things like fairness and privacy, and later added extra guidance specifically for generative AI (like ChatGPT-style tools). It's a recommended playbook, not an enforceable law, and each country can still make its own separate rules.

scope: all AI systems, continent-wide strategic guidance for AU's 55 member states — sets shared goals, not enforceable rules; implementation is left to individual countries
enforcement_mechanism: no — a strategy document, not a law; AU has no power to fine or license; enforcement (if any) would come from individual member states adopting their own laws
effective_date_or_status: Endorsed by the AU Executive Council 18-19 July 2024 in Accra, Ghana
plain_language_summary: African Union countries agreed on a shared game plan for developing AI in ways that benefit Africa — building skills, attracting investment, and managing risks — but this is a strategic roadmap, not a law, and each of the 55 member countries decides its own actual rules (most currently have none, see individual country rows).

region_or_country: Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) / Bletchley Declaration & AI Safety Summit process
key_instruments: Bletchley Declaration (Nov 2023, signed by 28 countries + EU); follow-on Seoul (2024) and Paris (2025) AI Safety Summits; Global Partnership on AI, which merged into the OECD in 2024
scope: advanced/'frontier' AI systems and general international AI-safety cooperation; not a comprehensive rulebook for everyday AI use
enforcement_mechanism: no — declarations and summit commitments with no fines or licensing; produced some shared outputs (e.g. a network of national AI Safety Institutes) but no binding enforcement
effective_date_or_status: Bletchley Declaration signed Nov 2023; Seoul Summit May 2024; Paris AI Action Summit Feb 2025; next GPAI Summit scheduled Bratislava, Slovakia, Nov 2025; GPAI formally merged into the OECD in 2024
plain_language_summary: This is a running series of international summits (UK, South Korea, France, and more to come) where countries agree, in writing, to cooperate on the risks of the most powerful 'frontier' AI models. It has produced shared statements and a network of AI safety research institutes, but no binding rules or penalties.

key_instruments: No comprehensive federal AI law; patchwork of binding state laws (Colorado AI Act, California AI transparency/employment laws, Illinois, Texas, Utah), sector-specific federal agency enforcement, and a Dec 2025 federal Executive Order ('Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence') aiming to preempt state laws
scope: varies hugely by state and sector — e.g. Colorado covers 'high-risk' AI used in consequential decisions (employment, credit, housing); California covers AI transparency and employment uses; no single law covers all AI nationally
enforcement_mechanism: yes at the state level in states with laws (state attorneys general enforcement, some private rights of action); federal enforcement is via existing agency authority (FTC, EEOC, etc.) applied to AI, not an AI-specific statute; a Dec 2025 federal executive order is trying to override/preempt state AI laws via a new DOJ litigation task force
effective_date_or_status: No comprehensive federal law as of Sept 2026; Colorado AI Act's replacement framework starts Jan 1, 2027; California AI Transparency Act operative Aug 2026; federal preemption executive order signed Dec 11, 2025, with legal fights over its validity ongoing
plain_language_summary: The US has no single national AI law. Instead, individual states like Colorado and California have passed their own binding rules — mostly about being transparent when AI is used in things like hiring or lending. In late 2025 the federal government tried to override those state laws with an executive order, and as of late 2026 that fight over who's in charge (states or the federal government) is still playing out in court.

key_instruments: No federal AI-specific statute (the proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, AIDA, died when Parliament was prorogued Jan 2025 and will not return); governance instead comes from federal privacy law (PIPEDA), Quebec's Law 25 (binding rules on automated decision-making), a voluntary federal Code of Conduct for generative AI, and sector-specific directives (financial services, government procurement, health tech)
scope: privacy and automated-decision-making aspects of AI are covered by binding law (mainly in Quebec); generative AI development is covered only by a voluntary code; no general cross-sector binding AI statute
enforcement_mechanism: yes for the privacy-law pieces (Quebec's privacy regulator can investigate and fine under Law 25); no enforcement for the voluntary generative-AI Code of Conduct
effective_date_or_status: AIDA formally abandoned; federal government tabled Bill C-36 (privacy reform) June 15, 2026, which does not revive AIDA; Canada launched a $2B, 5-year 'AI for All' National AI Strategy June 4, 2026 (investment/policy package, not a binding law)
plain_language_summary: Canada tried to pass a big national AI law but it died in Parliament in 2025 and the government has said it isn't coming back. Right now AI in Canada is governed by a patchwork: Quebec has real, enforceable privacy rules that cover automated decisions, the federal government only has a voluntary 'be responsible' code for AI companies, and there's a big new government investment strategy — but no binding, all-of-Canada AI law.

key_instruments: Bill PL 2338/2023 ('Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial') — a comprehensive, EU-AI-Act-inspired risk-based framework
scope: would cover all AI systems with a risk-tiered approach (banned practices, high-risk obligations); includes contested provisions requiring payment for copyrighted training data
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — bill includes proposed oversight/liability mechanisms but has not been enacted, so nothing is enforceable yet
effective_date_or_status: Approved by the Senate Dec 10, 2024; as of May 2026 still under review by a special committee in the Chamber of Deputies (House), with additional related bills introduced as recently as Feb 2026; no enactment date yet
plain_language_summary: Brazil has written a detailed, EU-style AI law and its Senate already approved it back in 2024, but it's still stuck in the lower house of Congress being debated and amended — including a controversial rule that would require AI companies to pay for the copyrighted material they train on. It is not yet in effect.

key_instruments: National Law to Regulate the Use of Artificial Intelligence (Senate bill introduced Feb 11, 2026, by Sen. Karina Ruíz); plus a narrower April 2026 reform to labor and copyright law covering AI use of performers' image/voice
scope: the pending comprehensive bill would cover public- and private-sector AI broadly, including bans on things like AI-driven lethal autonomous weapons and electoral deepfakes; the enacted labor/copyright reform covers only performers' image and voice rights
enforcement_mechanism: the labor/copyright reform (enacted April 2026) is binding; the comprehensive AI bill is not yet law so has no enforcement yet
effective_date_or_status: Comprehensive bill introduced to the Senate Feb 11, 2026, referred to committee, anticipated for further discussion in the Sept 2026 session — no enactment as of research date; separate labor/copyright AI reform passed the Chamber of Deputies April 7, 2026
plain_language_summary: Mexico doesn't have a general AI law yet, despite over 100 attempts at bills since 2020. A serious new comprehensive bill was introduced to the Senate in February 2026 and could be debated further in September 2026. Separately, Mexico already passed a narrower, real law in April 2026 protecting performers' faces and voices from being copied by AI without consent.

key_instruments: Federal: 'Recommendations for Reliable Artificial Intelligence' (Provision 2/2023) — non-binding ethical guidelines for national public administration; plus binding but narrow provincial rules in 4 provinces (Buenos Aires, Jujuy, Río Negro, San Juan) on ethical use/human oversight in public and judicial AI use
scope: federal guidelines cover AI use across the national public sector as voluntary recommendations; provincial rules are binding but limited to public/judicial-sector AI in those 4 provinces only, not private-sector AI nationally
enforcement_mechanism: no enforcement at the federal level (voluntary guidelines); provincial rules may carry binding force within their sector/jurisdiction, but no comprehensive national enforcement regime exists
effective_date_or_status: Federal recommendations issued June 1, 2023; provincial regulations in place as of early 2026; a new bill on 'cognitive autonomy' protecting minors from AI profiling was introduced Feb 20, 2026 and remains pending
plain_language_summary: Argentina has no binding national AI law — just voluntary ethical guidance for its own government agencies. A handful of provinces have made their own binding rules, but only for AI used in public services and courts, not for AI in general. A new bill to protect children from AI profiling was introduced in 2026 but hasn't passed.

key_instruments: AI Regulation Bill (Boletín N° 16.821-19), introduced by the Presidency May 2024 — an EU-AI-Act-style, risk-tiered bill
scope: would cover all AI systems (including foreign providers whose AI outputs reach Chilean users), with a risk classification system, bans on unacceptable-risk uses, and synthetic-content/deepfake labeling rules
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — bill is still in the legislative process (second constitutional review in the Senate as of 2026); separately, Chile's new comprehensive data-protection law (Ley 21.719, GDPR-style) becomes enforceable Dec 1, 2026 and will interact with AI systems that process personal data
effective_date_or_status: AI bill introduced May 2024, in second constitutional review in the Senate as of 2025/2026, not yet enacted; related Ley 21.719 (data protection, not AI-specific) takes effect Dec 1, 2026
plain_language_summary: Chile is working on its own EU-style AI law that would classify AI systems by risk level and require labeling of deepfakes, but it's still moving through the Senate and isn't law yet. A separate, unrelated new privacy law (not AI-specific) does take effect at the end of 2026 and will affect any AI system that handles personal data.

key_instruments: Bill 025 of 2026 (before the House of Representatives) and Statutory Bill 154 of 2024 — both propose comprehensive AI regulation with risk/impact assessments, transparency, human oversight, and a high-risk-system registry
scope: would cover developers, providers and deployers of AI systems broadly, with extra duties for systems affecting fundamental rights; a narrower binding rule (Resolution 1644 of 2026) already governs AI use in telemedicine specifically
enforcement_mechanism: not yet for the general bills (not enacted); the telemedicine resolution is binding and requires that clinical decisions stay with human professionals, who can accept/modify/reject AI recommendations
effective_date_or_status: Bill 025 of 2026 pending in the House as of research date; Statutory Bill 154 pending since 2024; Ministry of Health Resolution 1644 of 2026 on telemedicine AI already in force
plain_language_summary: Colombia doesn't have a general AI law yet, but two comprehensive bills are moving through Congress that would require companies to assess and disclose AI risks. In the meantime, Colombia already has one narrow binding rule in place: AI can suggest things in telemedicine, but a human doctor always has the final say.

key_instruments: Law No. 31814 (Law promoting the use of AI for economic and social development) + its implementing regulation, Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM
scope: applies broadly to AI development and use across public and private sectors, with obligations including impact assessments, human oversight, and technical documentation retention
enforcement_mechanism: yes — oversight from the Secretariat for Government and Digital Transformation (SGTD) and, for data-related aspects, the National Authority for Protection of Personal Data (ANPD); specific penalty amounts were not confirmed in this search and should be checked against the primary regulation text
effective_date_or_status: Law enacted 2023; implementing Supreme Decree published Sept 9, 2025; regulation entered into force Jan 22, 2026 (90 business days after publication); public-sector compliance deadline Sept 9, 2026; private-sector compliance phased over up to 4 years
plain_language_summary: Peru became the first country in Latin America with a real, general AI regulation now in force. Companies and government agencies using AI have to assess the risks, keep humans in the loop, and document what their systems do — government agencies had until September 2026 to comply, and private companies get up to 4 years to catch up. I could not confirm the exact fine amounts for breaking the rules, so that detail needs a follow-up check.
